title: Is there an AI that can find B-roll in my own footage?
summary: Find existing B-roll by describing the picture you need, choose between Premiere search and an assistant, and turn useful matches into an editable selection.
body_markdown:
## What you’ll take away


- Describe visible subjects and actions instead of only abstract moods.
- Start with Premiere for a direct lookup; consider an assistant for organized selections and follow-on work.
- Choose the shot for what it communicates beside the spoken line.


## Describe the missing picture


If an interviewee discusses packing an order, describe a person folding the box, placing the product inside, or sealing the package. Those are visible actions. “Customer satisfaction” is a broader idea that may return plausible but unhelpful images. Break the brief into pictures that communicate it.


Include framing when it matters: a wide view to establish the work area, a medium shot connecting a person to the task, or a close-up of their hands. Three beautiful details may leave the viewer unable to understand the action. Search for the role the picture must play in the sequence.


## Choose a search box or an assistant


[Adobe documents natural-language visual search in Premiere](https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/organize-media/file-organization/media-intelligence-and-search-panel.html) . If the material is already in your project and you need one shot, that is a sensible starting point. Another subscription is not necessary simply because you want to search pictures.


An assistant becomes interesting when the request includes more work: search a specified footage set, explain why candidates fit, collect them, and help prepare the edit. Wideframe’s[find-clips-visual recipe](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/find-clips-visual/) describes this search-and-collection task. Choose according to the work after retrieval, rather than assuming one product always finds better footage.


## An example: show how a product works


Imagine an illustrative reusable-bottle video with an interview, tabletop shots, and outdoor footage. The line is “the cap opens with one hand.” A useful search asks for a hand opening that cap. Someone carrying the bottle on a trail provides lifestyle context but does not demonstrate the mechanism.


Gather options with different roles: a clear view of the action, a detail, and a wider setup. Watch the whole movement rather than choosing one appealing frame. The viewer needs to understand what happens. If the action was never filmed, request a pickup or change the coverage plan instead of presenting a near match as proof.


## Give Wideframe a bounded footage job


Identify the folders or cameras, visible action, and desired output. You may want a bin of alternatives because the narration is still changing. Or you may already know the order and want candidates prepared for one passage. Include that distinction in the request.


The public skill page supplies instructions for adding and saving the workflow in Wideframe. Its described output includes time references and a reason for each match. Use those explanations to decide whether a shot demonstrates the action, sets the scene, or simply decorates it. The assistant gathers options; the editorial purpose determines which belongs.


## Make the picture work with the line


Choose the shot’s entry around the idea the viewer needs to see. Revealing the cap action too early can spend the visual payoff before the explanation. Holding the detail too long can slow the next sentence. Listen and watch together while choosing the range.


Consider neighboring shots too. A bottle may switch hands or colors between angles. Those differences change how smoothly and honestly the footage can be combined. A highly relevant result is not automatically the right cutaway for every position. Search creates choices; editing creates the relationship between them.


## Carry the selection into the next cut


Keep source references and enough surrounding material to revise timing. Wideframe’s[export-premiere workflow](https://try.wideframe.com/skills/export-premiere/) provides a path from selects or sequences to a Premiere project. The useful destination is material you can continue editing, not search hits you must reconstruct from memory.


Reuse the search workflow for the next product shoot, or return to unused candidates when the same video needs a shorter version. Our[B-roll assembly guide](https://try.wideframe.com/blog/how-to-assemble-b-roll-sequences-from-descriptions/) covers the wider process, and[semantic search explained](https://try.wideframe.com/blog/semantic-search-for-video-editing-explained/) introduces retrieval concepts. Start with one real coverage need and choose the tool that moves your footage into a useful editing state.
